newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya capital returns to normal after protest.
newsitem.headline: Kenya capital returns to normal after protest.

text.p: The Kenyan capital Nairobi returned to normal on Friday a day after opposition protest shut down the city on budget day.

Shops opened and traffic moved through the central business district with no sign of the massive security presence deployed on Thursday to prevent a march to parliament by the pro-reform National Convention Assembly (NCA).

Opposition MPs protesting at finance minister Musalia Mudavadi's budget scuffled in parliament with members of the ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) on Thursday in front of President Daniel arap Moi.
Outside parliament pro-KANU demonstrators, who said they were paid by the ruling party, forced the NCA to cancel a walk to parliament to present MPs with copies of two constitutional reform bills.
Paramilitary General Service Unit troops fought university students, while around 1,000 reformist protesters staged a march through Nairobi's deserted streets.
Despite the protest the Nairobi Stock Exchange and the interbank foreign exchange market traded normal volumes, dealers said.

"The market seems to have brushed what happened yesterday aside.Until yesterday we were still receiving orders for treasury bills from foreign investors, which is another proof that they still have confidence in our market," said a dealer.
The independent Nation newspaper argued in an editorial on Friday that Nairobi residents, whatever their views on reform, resented the threat of violence which disrupted business.

"The residents stayed away from their officies and other places of work becaue they feared for the safety of their lives and property. They want peace to conduct their business. That seems to be the bottom line," the newspaper said.

"City residents did not stay away from work becaue they are against reforms; but becaue they are against the methods being adopted by the reform lobby, which seeks confrontation. They are also upset with the government that refuses to listen to its citizens. This simply can't go on," it said.

President Moi, 73 this year, looks certain to extend his 19-year rule for another five years when elections are held later this year, because of the existing electoral rules and the deep personal and ethnic splits within the opposition.
The NCA, an alliance of opposition, church and civic groups demands a mininimum package of constitutional change before elections.
